power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Pre- and posttraumatic cognitions, coping, and PTSD symptoms (retrosp. survey)
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
This online study aims to shed more light on both risk and protective factors on a cognitive and behavioral level before and after having experienced a traumatic event. For this purpose, retrospective questions will be asked about assumptions and cognitive processing styles prior to and coping strategies directly after the trauma, respectively. In addition, measures of past and present distress related to the trauma will be collected as well as past and present trauma symptoms. 
The study covers two projects, both with distinct main research foci: One study focusses on investigating assumptions preceding the trauma (study A), and the other one on coping strategies following the trauma (study B). For better illustration, the planned projects will be presented separately, unless there are issues that concern both studies. 
Main research questions:
Study A (pre-traumatic factors): Are current levels of mental health (i.e., current distress from the specified trauma, current PTSD symptoms, levels of depression, anxiety, stress, and life satisfaction) associated with pre-traumatic levels of positive mental health, worthiness of self, self-worth, benevolence of the world, benevolence of people, and randomness?
Study B (post-traumatic factors): Are current levels of mental health (i.e., current distress from the specified trauma, current PTSD symptoms, levels of depression, anxiety, stress, and life satisfaction) associated with specific coping strategies following the traumatic event (i.e., problem and emotion focused vs. avoidant coping, coping flexibility, verbalization and imagination of the event, perceived social support)?
Additional: Are posttraumatic symptoms within the first month following the traumatic event associated with current PTSD symptoms?
table.design_dependent_variables:
Dependent variables that will be relevant in both studies:
1.) Current posttraumatic stress symptoms experienced during the last month, indexed via the PTSD checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5)
2.) Current life satisfaction measured by the Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS)
3.) Current and past distress from the specified trauma using a 10-point likert scale
4.) Current depressive, anxiety and stress symptoms assessed by the Depressions-Angst-Stress-Scale (DASS-21)
Study A pre-traumatic factors:
Positive mental health: Retrospectively measured via the Positive Mental Health Scale (PMH-scale), i.e., for the period of the 12 months prior to the traumatic event.
Assumptions about the world: Retrospectively measured with the World Assumptions Scale (WAS) for the period of the 12 months prior to the traumatic event (subscales: Self-worth*, self-controllability, luck, justice, controllability, randomness*, benevolence of people*, benevolence of world). These eight subscales can be summarized in three subscales: worthiness of self*, meaningfulness of the world, and benevolence of the world*. The variables marked with an * will be those relevant for the main analyses.
Study B post-traumatic factors:
Coping-strategies: Retrospectively measured with the Coping Orientation to Problems Experienced Inventory (Brief-COPE), i.e., within the first month following the traumatic event.
Verbalization and imagination of the traumatic event following the trauma: Retrospectively measured on a 4 point likert-scale, assessment of frequency of several types of verbalization (5 items), strategies during verbalization (7 items and one open question asking for individual strategies), frequency of intended imagination (1 item), strategies during imagination (6 items). All scales were developed by the research team for the purpose of the present study.
Social support: Retrospectively measured by one self-created item assessing sought and received social support.
Relevant variables across both projects:
Demographic data: age, gender, education
Trauma history: The Life Event Checklist (LEC) will be applied to assess the sample's general trauma experiences. However, in order to be eligible to participate in the study, there must be one trauma that happened during the past 18 months. Participants have to indicate what type of trauma this was (using the LEC classification), their role during the trauma (self-experienced, observed, not involved), and its' frequency. This trauma will then serve as index trauma for answering the study's questions. In case a participant experienced multiple traumas during the past 18 months, they will be asked to select the most distressing one.
Posttraumatic stress symptoms: Retrospectively measured within the first month after the trauma (one question per DSM-5 symptom cluster, self-made scale).
table.study_design_overview: There will be no conditions since this is a cross-sectional online study. Exclusion criteria: current psychiatric disease, being under 18 years, and not having experienced a traumatic event in the past 18 months.
table.statistical_tests:
For both projects, correlational analyses will be conducted to examine the main research questions. Results of the correlation analyses will then serve as a foundation for more fine-tuned follow-up analyses, i.e., regression analyses. Only variables that correlated significantly with the dependent variables will be considered. Alpha level of .05 will be used for all analyses. 
Study A pre-traumatic factors:
-	Correlational analyses: positive mental health, worthiness of self, self-worth, benevolence of the world, benevolence of people, randomness and current levels of PTSD symptoms and current distress from the specified trauma and current levels of depression, anxiety, stress, and life satisfaction. 
-	Multiple regression analyses: predicting current PTSD symptoms using the pre-traumatic factors (positive mental health, worthiness of self, self-worth, benevolence of the world, benevolence of people, randomness) as predictors that correlated with current PCL-5 scores, while simultaneously controlling for general variables (e.g., age and gender). Further analyses will be conducted predicting current distress and current levels of depression, anxiety, stress, and life satisfaction, using the same rational as for the regression predicting PTSD symptoms. 
Study B post-traumatic factors:
-	Correlational analyses: emotion focused coping, problem focused coping, avoidant coping, coping flexibility, verbalization, imagination, social support, life satisfaction, current burden from the event, current PTSD symptoms, and current levels of depression, anxiety, stress
-	Multiple regression analyses: predicting current PTSD symptoms using post-traumatic factors (e.g. emotion focused coping, problem focused coping, avoidant coping, coping flexibility, verbalization, imagination and social support) that correlated with current PCL-5 scores.
Relevant for both studies:
-	Correlation analysis: PTSD symptoms within the first month following the traumatic event and current PTSD symptoms.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Results from participants who did not finish the survey will be excluded. Outliers (e.g., with extreme data points such as > 3 SDs from the sample's mean for a certain variable) will be inspected, and all analyses will be run with and without these outliers. We will also check the data to try to identify participants who may not have complied with the study's instructions (e.g., questionnaires were completed very quickly) and will repeat all analyses with and without these participants. In case of not normally distributed data the data will be transformed.
table.sample_size: We are planning to include N = 280 participants.
table.additional_comments: Study B Post-traumatic factors: The specific strategies participants report following the traumatic event (i.e., verbalization and/or imagination) will be investigated more detailed in an exploratory analysis, e.g., correlation analyses between the use of specific strategies and indicators of current mental health will be conducted. Additional multiple regression analyses will be conducted to further specify the correlational data.

table.title: Trauma type, coping strategies, and trauma symptoms in the context of PTSD
table.existing_data_explanation: It's complicated. We have already collected some data but explain in Question 8 why readers may consider this a valid pre-registration nevertheless.
table.research_questions:
The primary aim of the original online study (aspredicted ID: #107000) was to examine risk and protective factors before and after having experienced a traumatic event. To do so, retrospective questions about e.g., pre-trauma, cognitive processing styles were included as well as questions about coping strategies post-trauma. In addition, measures of past and present distress related to the trauma and trauma-symptoms were applied. 
Via secondary analyses we will now examine the specific role of the different types of trauma participants experienced. Specifically, we will examine the relationship between different types of trauma, coping strategies, and trauma-relevant symptomatology. To do so, participants will be classified into two groups: those who have experienced an interpersonal trauma vs. those who have experienced a non-interpersonal trauma. First, we will examine whether people differ in terms of coping strategies used, e.g., whether people use dysfunctional coping strategies (i.e., avoidant coping) more often after having experienced interpersonal compared to non-interpersonal trauma. Second, differences between types of trauma in post-traumatic, depressive, anxiety, and stress symptoms as well as in life satisfaction will be examined. Third, correlational analyses will be employed, per trauma type, examining possible relationships between coping strategies used and symptoms.
table.design_dependent_variables:
1. Coping strategies measured via the Coping Orientation to Problems Experienced Inventory (Brief-COPE), i.e., participants were asked to complete the Brief-COPE while thinking back to the first month following the traumatic event.
2. Current posttraumatic stress symptoms (i.e., during the last month) measured via the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5).
3. Current depressive, anxiety and stress symptoms (i.e., during the last week) measured via the Depression-Anxiety-Stress-Scale-21 (DASS-21).
4. Current life satisfaction (i.e., during the last month) measured via the Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS).
Other relevant variables:
- Demographic data: age, gender, education
table.study_design_overview:
The study was a cross-sectional online study without any (experimental) conditions. The study included participants aged 18 years or older who had experienced a traumatic life event in the previous 18 months. Participant's trauma history was measured via the Life Events Checklist (LEC-5), i.e., participants had to indicate what type of trauma they had experienced, their role during the trauma (self-experienced, observed, not involved), and its' frequency. This information then served as the index trauma for answering the study's questions. If participants had experienced multiple traumas during the previous 18 months, they were asked to select the most distressing one. For the purpose of the present secondary analyses, the LEC's items will be retrospectively classified into two categories, describing an interpersonal trauma, i.e., trauma caused by other people, and describing a non-interpersonal trauma, i.e., trauma caused by an accident, natural or medical factor, to enable us to compare different trauma types. 
Additional information: In the original pre-registration, it was planned to exclude participants with a current psychiatric disease. This criterion was adjusted during data collection, such that the final sample also includes participants who currently experience psychological symptoms.
table.statistical_tests:
Independent samples t-tests, independent variable: interpersonal trauma versus non-interpersonal trauma:
1. Coping strategies: sum score of the subscales constituting emotion focused coping, problem focused coping, and avoidant coping assessed via the Brief-COPE
2. Trauma symptoms: total sum score of the PCL-5 
3. Depressive, anxiety, and stress symptoms: sum score of the subscales depression, anxiety, and stress assessed via the DASS-21
4. Life satisfaction: total sum score of the SWLS

Correlational analyses, separated for the two trauma types, among the following variables: each coping strategy (emotion focused coping, problem focused coping, avoidant coping), levels of current PTSD symptoms, depression, anxiety, and stress, and levels of current life satisfaction.

Two multiple hierarchical regression analyses, separated for the two trauma types: predicting current PTSD symptoms using age and gender as predictors in the first step and adding the three coping strategies (emotion focused coping, problem focused coping, avoidant coping) as predictors in the second step.

One multiple hierarchical regression analysis, across both trauma types: predicting current PTSD symptoms using age and gender as predictors in the first step and adding trauma type as predictor in the second step.
 
Alpha level of .05 will be used for all analyses.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: The definition and handling of outliers and the rules for excluding observations will be the same as described in the original pre-registration.
table.sample_size: Data collection was stopped at N = 488. In the original pre-registration, it was planned to include N = 280 participants. However, during the course of the study, many participants didn't complete the survey or didn't meet the inclusion criteria. Hence, in order to achieve the a priori planned sample size for the data analysis of N = 280, the study continued longer. Given the online data collection, however, it was not possible to exactly terminate the data collection when the planned sample size was reached, and thus more participants completed the survey. Due to the exclusion of participants who did not finish the survey (N = 92) or did not meet the inclusion criteria (N = 96), the final sample for the present secondary analyses includes N = 300.
table.additional_comments: Data has been collected already, and the present pre-registration describes secondary analyses of these data. The data that will be re-analyzed are part of the original study entitled "Pre- and posttraumatic cognitions, coping, and PTSD symptoms (retrosp. survey)", which were pre-registered on aspredicted on 14th September 2022 with the following ID: #107000. The secondary analyses that are registered in this present pre-registration are novel and do not overlap with the research questions and hypothesis included in the primary pre-registration. In addition, the principal investigator of the secondary analyses did not review the data yet.

text.formatted: In our recent study <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Hartmann et al., 2026)</ref> we investigated the relationship between trauma type, coping style, and posttraumatic symptomatology in a retrospective online sample of individuals who had experienced a traumatic life event within the past 18 months.

text.text: Findings highlighted avoidant coping as a factor associated with differences in posttraumatic symptomatology across trauma types (i.e., interpersonal vs. non-interpersonal trauma).
Specifically, participants who had experienced interpersonal trauma reported significantly higher levels of avoidant coping than those who had experienced non-interpersonal trauma.

Moreover, avoidant coping explained a significant proportion of variance in posttraumatic stress symptoms within both trauma groups, and trauma type itself accounted for significant unique variance in posttraumatic stress symptoms across the entire sample.

Finally, an exploratory mediation analysis indicated that avoidant coping statistically accounted for the association between trauma type and posttraumatic symptoms, consistent with a partial statistical mediation.
